title: Ἀνὴρ καὶ γυνὴ ⟨ἀργαλέα⟩
titleEn: The Man and His Ill-Tempered Wife
part: The Man and His Ill-Tempered Wife (Chambry 49 · Perry 95)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 49 (= Perry 95). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔχων τις γυναῖκα πρὸς πάντας τοὺς οἰκείους λίαν τὸ ἦθος ἀργαλέαν ἠβουλήθη γνῶναι εἰ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς πατρῴους οἰκέτας ὁμοίως διάκειται· ὅθεν μετὰ προφάσεως εὐλόγου πρὸς τὸν πατέρα αὐτὴν ἔπεμψε.
sentences.tr: Echōn tis gynaika pros pantas tous oikeious lian to ēthos argalean ēboulēthē gnōnai ei kai pros tous patrōious oiketas homoiōs diakeitai· hothen meta prophaseōs eulogou pros ton patera autēn epempse.
sentences.l: Someone, having a wife exceedingly harsh in character toward all the household, wished to know whether she was disposed in the same way toward her father's servants as well; whence, with a plausible pretext, he sent her to her father.
sentences.i: A man whose wife was exceedingly hard on everyone in the house wanted to know whether she behaved the same way toward her father's servants; and so, on a plausible excuse, he sent her back to her father.
sentences.n: τὸ ἦθος is an accusative of respect — harsh 'in respect of her character'. εἰ … διάκειται is an indirect question after γνῶναι, and Greek keeps the tense the thought had when it was thought (present indicative) where English shifts it back. οἰκεῖοι are the people of the house, οἰκέται the household slaves. εὐλόγου is 'plausible, specious' — a pretext that will pass, not a good reason.

sentences.t: Μετὰ δὲ ὀλίγας ἡμέρας ἀνελθούσης αὐτῆς ἐπυνθάνετο πῶς αὐτὴν οἱ οἰκεῖοι προσεδέξαντο.
sentences.tr: Meta de oligas hēmeras anelthousēs autēs epynthaneto pōs autēn hoi oikeioi prosedexanto.
sentences.l: And after a few days, she having come back, he inquired how the household had received her.
sentences.i: A few days later, when she had come back, he asked how the household had received her.
sentences.n: ἀνελθούσης αὐτῆς is a genitive absolute — a noun and participle standing apart from the main clause to set the scene. It is the commonest way these fables move from one moment to the next.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ εἰπούσης· « Οἱ βουκόλοι καὶ οἱ ποιμένες με ὑπεβλέποντο, » ἔφη πρὸς αὐτήν· « Ἀλλ’ ὦ γύναι, εἰ τούτοις ἀπήχθου οἱ ὄρθρου μὲν τὰς ποίμνας ἐξελαύνουσιν, ὀψὲ δὲ εἰσίασι, τί χρὴ προσδοκᾶν περὶ τούτων οἷς πᾶσαν τὴν ἡμέραν συνδιέτριβες ; »
sentences.tr: Tēs de eipousēs· « Hoi boukoloi kai hoi poimenes me hypebleponto, » ephē pros autēn· « All’ ō gynai, ei toutois apēchthou hoi orthrou men tas poimnas exelaunousin, opse de eisiasi, ti chrē prosdokan peri toutōn hois pasan tēn hēmeran syndietribes ; »
sentences.l: And when she said: « The cowherds and the shepherds looked at me from under their brows, » he said to her: « But, woman, if you made yourself hateful to these men, who drive the flocks out at daybreak and come in late, what must one expect concerning those with whom you spent the whole day? »
sentences.i: When she said: « The cowherds and the shepherds gave me black looks, » he said to her: « But, woman, if you made yourself hateful even to these men — who drive the flocks out at dawn and do not come in till evening — what is one to expect of the people you spent the whole day with? »
sentences.n: Τῆς δὲ εἰπούσης is another genitive absolute, with the bare article doing the work of a pronoun ('and when she said'); ὁ δέ, ἡ δέ for 'and he, and she' runs through every fable. ὑπεβλέποντο, 'looked at from under the brows', is the sidelong look of suspicion or dislike. ἀπήχθου is aorist of ἀπεχθάνομαι, 'to make oneself hated by' someone, with the dative — she is the one who gave the offence. ὄρθρου μέν … ὀψὲ δέ sets dawn against evening: these are the men least in the house, and even they could not bear her.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλάκις ἐκ τῶν μικρῶν τὰ μεγάλα καὶ ἐκ τῶν προδήλων τὰ ἄδηλα γνωρίζονται.
sentences.tr: Houtō pollakis ek tōn mikrōn ta megala kai ek tōn prodēlōn ta adēla gnōrizontai.
sentences.l: Thus often the great things are recognized from the small, and the unclear from the plain.
sentences.i: Thus it often happens that great matters are known from small ones, and hidden things from what is plain to see.
sentences.n: Οὕτω πολλάκις, 'thus often' — a closing hinge of the same family as οὕτω καί, 'so too'. γνωρίζονται is passive: the things are recognized. The neuter plurals τὰ μεγάλα, τὰ ἄδηλα are abstractions: 'the great things', 'the things not in view'.
